_comment: Curated external resources per module. Resources are CONTEXTUAL, not bookmarks: every entry names the lesson it supports and the moment to open it. Fields — 'lesson': a slug from src/content/modules/*.mdx, or null when it belongs to the module generally. 'when': before (warm up) | during (see it for real at a specific beat) | after (now that you've built it) | stuck (a SECOND explanation in another voice, surfaced after two failed runs) | further (optional depth on the module page). 'minutes': realistic read/watch time. 'adds': what this gives that the lesson cannot — not a summary. 'thumb': local '/thumbs/<slug>.webp' for type video only (forward declaration; the image assets land in a later phase), null otherwise. Third-party block editors and simulators are ALWAYS 'further' — never offered inline mid-lesson, because they are competing products. 'published' = the source's own date (best known; approximate for continuously-updated wikis and documentation roots); 'checked' = last verification. An entry whose link a human still has to supply carries 'url': null plus 'status': "needs-url" — it must never be rendered as a link. The monthly freshness workflow proposes edits via PR (lychee verifies liveness; the LLM only proposes; zod + this allowlist validate).

m1.title: How do ROBOTS work? — Argo's World (STEM for kids & teens)
m1.why: Friendly sense-think-act tour with zero assumed knowledge — matches lesson 1's framing exactly.
m1.adds: Shows real machines running sense-decide-act before you touch the simulator, so the loop reads as a fact about the world rather than a rule this app invented.

m1.title: Robot — Wikipedia
m1.why: A wide, plainly-written survey of what counts as a robot, readable straight after the first lesson.
m1.adds: Sets the one robot you just met beside factory arms, rovers and surgical arms, so 'robot' stops meaning 'the thing on my screen'.

m1.title: Light-emitting diode — Wikipedia
m1.why: The physical story behind the block you just switched on and off.
m1.adds: Explains why a real LED only lets current through one way — the lesson makes it blink, this says what is actually happening inside it.

m1.title: Turtle graphics — Wikipedia
m1.why: The same forward-and-turn idea told as drawing rather than driving — a fresh angle when the target pad keeps getting missed.
m1.adds: Re-teaches steering as a pen tracing a path on paper, a completely different mental picture for the same move-then-turn plan.

m1.title: Blockly Games — puzzle your way into blocks
m1.why: Free extra reps with the same block style our editor uses; Maze level pairs perfectly with Module 1.
m1.adds: Optional drilling on block-snapping muscle memory in a separate editor — worth a look once Module 1 is finished, not while you are in it.

m2.title: For loop — Wikipedia
m2.why: Warms up the repeat idea with the word professionals use for it, before the zig-zag mission asks for one.
m2.adds: Shows the same repeat block written as text code in half a dozen real languages, so the block reads as a translation rather than a toy.

m2.title: BBC micro:bit coding in 60 seconds — Creating Loops (Kitronik)
m2.why: Sixty seconds, spoken aloud, showing a loop block being built — the fastest possible second opinion after a failed run.
m2.adds: Says the loop idea out loud while the blocks move on screen, a different channel entirely from the lesson's written explanation, and it is over before frustration can build.

m2.title: Persistence of vision — Wikipedia
m2.why: Why a fast enough blink stops looking like a blink — the trick behind every screen and light show.
m2.adds: Answers the question the light show provokes but never addresses: what happens to your pattern once you shorten the wait past the point your eyes can follow.

m2.title: Iteration & Looping — MakeCode CS Intro course
m2.why: A full teaching unit on iteration, written for classrooms, if one module's worth of loops left you wanting more.
m2.adds: Separates the loop family — repeat, forever, while, for — into distinct tools with worked demos, where this module only ships the counted one.

m2.title: Control flow — Wikipedia
m2.why: The whole family of order-changing constructs, of which the repeat block is one member.
m2.adds: Maps out the loops, branches and jumps you have not met yet, so Module 2's single loop gets a visible place in a bigger system.

m2.title: Blockly Games: Maze (loops in action)
m2.why: Ten escalating loop puzzles — ideal optional practice after the zig-zag mission.
m2.adds: Ten more loop puzzles at rising difficulty, for when the module's two missions were not enough repetitions to make loops feel automatic.

m3.title: Sensor — Wikipedia
m3.why: A short warm-up on what a sensor is before the green distance block appears.
m3.adds: Shows that every sensor — heat, light, tilt, distance — does the one job of turning part of the world into a number, which is the move the whole lesson depends on.

m3.title: How Do Ultrasonic Distance Sensors Work? — The Learning Circuit
m3.why: Watch this at the moment the faint sensor ray first appears on the robot's nose.
m3.adds: Puts a real sensor on a bench and measures with it, so you see where the distance number comes from — a chirp, an echo and a stopwatch — which the simulator hands you for free and never shows.

m3.title: Conditional (computer programming) — Wikipedia
m3.why: The if-block, generalised, once you have dropped a sensor reading into one.
m3.adds: Introduces else, else-if and switch — the branches the lesson's single if-block hints at but does not hand you yet.

m3.title: Circuit 3B: Distance Sensor — SparkFun Inventor's Kit Guide
m3.why: The same stop-before-you-hit-it problem, walked through step by step in a different voice, for a learner whose wall-stop run keeps failing.
m3.adds: Works the threshold logic in the opposite direction — real wiring first, then the comparison that acts on the reading — so the idea arrives from the hardware side instead of the block side.

m3.title: Arduino Documentation — official docs
m3.why: The canonical reference for the boards and sensors this module simulates.
m3.adds: Shows what reading a real distance sensor actually costs you — pins, timing, libraries — none of which the green block makes you think about.

m3.title: Wokwi — free in-browser Arduino & MicroPython simulator
m3.why: See a REAL ultrasonic distance sensor wired to a simulated board — the grown-up version of our green sensor block.
m3.adds: Lets you wire the grown-up version of the green block yourself, with real pins and real code — a separate simulator, so save it for after the module.

m4.title: What is a Circuit? — SparkFun
m4.why: The classic illustrated circuits explainer, with a live current-flow simulation link. Old but definitive.
m4.adds: Hands you a current-flow simulation you can poke and deliberately break, which a page of prose about loops of electricity cannot.

m4.title: Ohm's law — Wikipedia
m4.why: Turns the water-hose analogy into the one equation that lets you predict a circuit instead of just describing it.
m4.adds: Makes voltage and current calculable rather than merely nameable, which is the step from understanding a circuit to designing one.

m4.title: Gears — how do they work? (Explain That Stuff)
m4.why: Plain-English speed-vs-torque explanation with everyday examples; recently updated.
m4.adds: Walks through several real gear trains — clocks, drills, bikes — so the speed-for-strength trade stops being one bicycle sentence.

m4.title: Gears Explained — mechanical engineering (video)
m4.why: Clear animated gear-ratio and torque walkthrough if the article's diagrams aren't enough.
m4.adds: Animates the teeth actually meshing and counting round, which is the part static diagrams lose and the exact part that makes a gear ratio click.

m4.title: Electric motor — Wikipedia
m4.why: What is inside the thing the gears are bolted to, once you know why the gears are there at all.
m4.adds: Joins this module's two halves — it is the piece showing electricity becoming the spin that gears then trade away for strength.

m4.title: Adafruit Learn — build guides for real parts
m4.why: A deep, beginner-friendly library of wiring and soldering guides for the parts in this module.
m4.adds: Turns this module's concepts into shopping lists and step-by-step wiring photos, for when you want one of these on the desk in front of you.

m5.title: Event-driven programming — Wikipedia
m5.why: Names the shift from 'runs top to bottom' to 'waits and responds' just before the hat block introduces it.
m5.adds: Shows that the hat block is how nearly all real software is organised — apps, games, websites — and not a robot-only convention.

m5.title: Mobile robot — Wikipedia
m5.why: The category your obstacle-course robot belongs to, read while you are still building it.
m5.adds: Lays out the navigation strategies real robots choose between, which is useful precisely while you are inventing your own for the maze.

m5.title: How Engineering Robots Works — Crash Course Engineering #33
m5.why: A brisk, well-produced retelling of sensors, control and actuators as one machine — the second voice to reach for when the final mission will not come together.
m5.adds: Re-explains the whole sense-decide-act loop from an engineer's angle rather than a programmer's, which is often the framing that unsticks a program that is failing for reasons the blocks do not show.

m5.title: Debugging — Wikipedia
m5.why: Puts a name and a method to the thing you just spent an hour doing.
m5.adds: Turns the trial and error you just lived through into a named, repeatable technique you can reach for deliberately next time.

m5.title: micro:bit — the real board behind these blocks
m5.why: The official home of the pocket-sized board whose event model this module borrows.
m5.adds: Shows the physical board — buttons, shake, sound — whose events these hat blocks are modelled on, and what it costs to actually own one.

m5.title: micro:bit MakeCode — events playground
m5.why: Blocks with MANY event hats (button A, shake, sound) plus a built-in simulator — the bridge to real hardware.
m5.adds: Offers far more event hats than this course ships and downloads straight to real hardware — a separate editor, so open it after the module, never during.

go-physical.title: Wokwi — keep simulating while you wait for parts
go-physical.why: The doc's promise kept: the simulator path stays open if hardware isn't accessible yet.
go-physical.adds: Keeps the hands-on path open while the parts are still in the post, so a shipping delay never becomes a stopped course.
